title: Secretary Problem Variants & Extensions
text:
The classical secretary problem is only the starting point.
Changing the information available, the objective, the number of choices, or the horizon leads to genuinely different optimal-stopping problems.

title: Secretary Problem Variants & Extensions
text:
The classical benchmark
There are \(n\) candidates whose absolute ranks form a uniformly random permutation of
\[
1,2,\ldots,n,
\]
with rank \(1\) best. Write \(X_k\) for the absolute rank of the candidate arriving at position \(k\), and \(R_k\) for that candidate’s relative rank among the first \(k\) arrivals.
Candidates are observed sequentially. At time \(k\), only the candidate’s relative rank among the first \(k\) observations is known. Decisions are irrevocable, and only one candidate may be selected.
The objective is
\[
\max_{\tau}\Pr(X_\tau=1).
\]
For a threshold \(1\le r<n\), reject the first \(r\) candidates and then accept the first subsequent record. Its success probability is
\[
P_n(r)
=
\frac{r}{n}
\sum_{j=r+1}^{n}\frac{1}{j-1}.
\]
For \(r=0\), the first candidate is selected immediately and \(P_n(0)=1/n\).
As \(n\to\infty\), a choice of optimal threshold \(r_n^\star\) satisfies
\[
\frac{r_n^\star}{n}\to \frac1e,
\]
and the optimal success probability also converges to \(1/e\).
The extensions below can be organized by asking which part of this benchmark is changed.

title: Secretary Problem Variants & Extensions
text:
1. Full-information secretary problem

Problem
Instead of seeing only relative ranks, suppose the numerical observations
\[
Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}F
\]
are revealed sequentially, where \(F\) is a known continuous distribution. Here \(Y_k\) is an observed value, not the absolute rank \(X_k\) used in the classical model.
The objective is to maximize
\[
\Pr\!\left(Y_\tau=\max_{1\le j\le n}Y_j\right).
\]


What changes?
The numerical value of the current observation contains information about how likely future observations are to exceed it.
The optimal decision therefore depends not only on whether the current observation is a record, but also on how large that record is.


Optimal-strategy structure
Using the probability-integral transform,
\[
U_i=F(Y_i),
\]
the problem can be reduced to independent \(U(0,1)\) observations.
The optimal rule is described by time-dependent critical values: a record is accepted only when its value is sufficiently large relative to the number of observations remaining.


Interactive first-decision experiment (uniform observations)
To obtain closed-form, verifiable stopping decisions, the experiment uses \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}U(0,1)\) with \(n=2\) or \(n=3\). After seeing the first value \(x\), accepting wins with probability \(x^{n-1}\).
Rejecting and then acting optimally has probability
\[
C_2(x)=1-x,
\]
and
\[
C_3(x)=
\begin{cases}
\frac34-\frac{x^2}{2},&0\le x\le\frac12,\\
\frac12+x-\frac{3x^2}{2},&\frac12<x\le1.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(n=3\), if the first value \(x\) is rejected, the second observation \(y\) should be accepted only if it is a record and \(y\ge 1/2\); otherwise the last observation is chosen only when it sets a new record. Integrating over the second observation gives \(C_3(x)\) above.
Thus the first-observation acceptance thresholds are \(1/2\) for \(n=2\) and \((1+\sqrt6)/5\approx0.68990\) for \(n=3\). These are first-stage thresholds, not the full-information rule for an arbitrary horizon.

    Continue optimally

Connection to the classical model
Both problems seek the overall maximum.
The difference is informational:

no information: only relative ranks are observed;
full information: the actual values are observed.

Gilbert and Mosteller developed the foundational analysis of both settings (Gilbert and Mosteller (1966)).

title: Secretary Problem Variants & Extensions
section: 2. The postdoc problem: selecting the second best
text:
2. The postdoc problem: selecting the second best

Problem
Change the reward from selecting absolute rank \(1\) to selecting absolute rank \(2\):
\[
\max_{\tau}\Pr(X_\tau=2).
\]
The arrival order is still uniformly random, decisions remain irrevocable, and only relative ranks are observed.


What changes?
The current record is no longer the only potentially useful candidate: a candidate with current relative rank \(2\) can also be the overall second best. Relative ranks \(a\ge3\) have zero immediate success probability. Thus changing the reward changes the stopping decisions that must be compared, even though the observed relative-rank information remains the same.


Interactive postdoc decision (exact backward induction)
Conditional on observing relative rank \(a\) at position \(k\), the probability that the current candidate has absolute rank \(2\) is
\[
g_{n,k}(a)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{k(n-k)}{n(n-1)},&a=1,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{k(k-1)}{n(n-1)},&a=2,\\[4pt]
0,&a\ge3.
\end{cases}
\]
The relative ranks are independent with \(R_k\) uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Let \(V_{n+1}=0\) and let \(V_k\) be the maximum probability of selecting absolute rank \(2\) before observing relative rank \(R_k\). Then
\[
V_k=\frac1k\sum_{a=1}^k\max\{g_{n,k}(a),V_{k+1}\},
\qquad k=n,n-1,\ldots,1.
\]
At position \(k\), select when \(g_{n,k}(a)\ge V_{k+1}\) and this success probability is positive; otherwise continue. When tied at zero, the experiment displays continuation. This dynamic program optimizes over all admissible decisions based on observed relative ranks.

    Candidates (n): 10
    
    Current position (k): 5
    
    Observed relative rank (a): 2
    
  
  
    Select now 
    Continue optimally 
  
  Optimal win probability before the first candidate:

Connection to the classical model
The information structure is unchanged. Only the reward changes:
\[
\mathbf 1_{\{X_\tau=1\}}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\mathbf 1_{\{X_\tau=2\}}.
\]
This makes the postdoc problem a particularly useful example of how the optimal rule can change when the target rank changes. For further analysis of the standard postdoc problem and its relationship to best-or-worst selection, see Bayón et al. (2018).

title: Secretary Problem Variants & Extensions
text:
3. Multiple-choice and dowry problems

Problem
Suppose the decision maker is allowed more than one selection.
With \(m\) available choices, the decision maker chooses stopping times
\[
\tau_1<\tau_2<\cdots<\tau_m.
\]
The success event depends on the particular model—for example, whether one of the selected observations is the overall best, or whether several top ranks must be captured.


Sakaguchi’s contribution
Sakaguchi’s work is an important early part of this branch of the literature.
His 1978 paper, Dowry Problems and OLA Policies (Sakaguchi (1978)), studied secretary-type stopping rules in a dowry formulation and belongs to the development of multiple-stopping extensions.
Sakaguchi also studied generalized secretary models with uncertain employment, showing that changing the selection mechanism itself can produce new optimal-stopping structures.


Tamaki’s double-choice problems
Tamaki subsequently analyzed explicit two-choice secretary problems.
In one formulation, the decision maker is allowed two choices and succeeds when one of them is the best or second-best candidate (Tamaki (1979a)). In another, the objective is to select both the maximum and the second maximum (Tamaki (1979b)).
These problems illustrate why multiple-choice secretary models require more state information than the classical one-choice problem.


Dynamic-programming structure
If \(j\) selections remain at time \(k\), the state must record both the information observed so far and the remaining number of choices.
Schematically,
\[
V_{k,j}(s)
=
\max\{
\text{value of selecting now},
\text{value of continuing}
\}.
\]
Selecting now changes the state from \(j\) remaining choices to \(j-1\).


Connection to the classical model
The classical secretary problem is recovered when
\[
m=1.
\]
Thus multiple-choice models enlarge the stopping problem by adding a resource variable: the number of selections still available.

title: Secretary Problem Variants & Extensions
text:
4. Unknown or random horizon

Problem
The classical model assumes that the total number \(n\) of observations is known.
Suppose instead that the number of observations is a random variable
\[
N.
\]
The distribution of \(N\) may be known even though its realized value is not.


What changes?
With a fixed horizon, the decision maker knows exactly how many observations remain.
With a random horizon, the continuation value must also account for the probability that the sequence ends.
The resulting continuation values must account for both the information observed and the conditional distribution of the remaining horizon.


Connection to the \(1/e\) phenomenon
The classical \(1/e\) threshold is not a universal rule for random horizons. In the continuous-time unified-approach model of Bruss (1984), a \(1/e\) law holds under the model’s specific conditional-independence assumptions. A generic prior distribution for the unknown horizon \(N\) need not yield the same optimal rule or success probability (Bruss (1984)).

title: Secretary Problem Variants & Extensions
section: 5. Last-success problems and the odds theorem
text:
5. Last-success problems and the odds theorem

Problem
Let
\[
I_1,\ldots,I_n
\]
be independent Bernoulli random variables with
\[
\Pr(I_k=1)=p_k,\qquad 0\le p_k<1.
\]
The objective is to stop at an index \(\tau\) for which \(I_\tau=1\) and no later success occurs. If there is no success, the attempt fails. Assume decisions use only the observations up to the current index.
Define
\[
q_k=1-p_k>0,
\qquad
r_k=\frac{p_k}{q_k}.
\]
Sum-the-odds rule (Bruss, 2000). Define
\[
s=\max\left(\{1\}\cup\left\{k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\sum_{j=k}^{n}r_j\ge1\right\}\right).
\]
Reject observations before \(s\), then stop at the first success \(I_k=1\) with \(k\ge s\). If no success occurs after \(s\), the attempt fails. When the total sum of odds is less than \(1\), this convention gives \(s=1\). This rule maximizes the probability of stopping on the last success among all stopping times in this model. See Bruss (2000).


Connection to secretary problems
The odds theorem is not the classical secretary problem itself.
It belongs to the same broader optimal-stopping family: the decision maker must act without knowing whether a future event will supersede the current one.

title: Secretary Problem Variants & Extensions
text:
6. Applicant-side secretary problems

Problem
The classical problem is posed from the employer’s perspective:

When should the employer stop?

Glass (2012) studied the problem from the applicant’s perspective (Glass (2012)).
Suppose the employer follows a known stopping rule and an applicant may choose an interview position \(i\).
The applicant seeks to maximize
\[
\Pr(\text{selected}\mid\text{position }i).
\]


What changes?
The applicant’s decision variable is an interview position \(i\), not the employer’s stopping time \(\tau\). The employer’s stopping rule is taken as given when the applicant chooses their position.


Known self-rank
If the applicant knows their own absolute rank, the best position can depend strongly on that rank.
This produces a strategic positioning problem built on top of a classical secretary stopping rule.

title: Secretary Problem Variants & Extensions
text:
7. Uncertain self-rank
Suppose the applicant does not know their absolute rank.
Let
\[
J\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
\]
be the applicant’s random absolute rank, distinct from the observed relative ranks \(R_k\), with a prior distribution. Assume the employer follows a specified stopping rule. For example, a truncated geometric prior is
\[
\Pr(J=j)
=
\frac{(1-q)q^{j-1}}{1-q^n},
\qquad 0<q<1.
\]
The applicant’s value from position \(i\) becomes
\[
V(i)
=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\Pr(J=j)
\Pr(\text{selected}\mid J=j,\text{position }i).
\]
This turns applicant positioning into a Bayesian decision problem under the specified employer stopping rule.

section: A map of the secretary-problem family
text:
A map of the secretary-problem family
The main extensions can be classified according to which component of the classical model is changed.


  
    Secretary Problem
  

  

    
      Information

      Full values
      Partial information
      Uncertain self-rank
    

    
      Objective
      Best candidate
      Second best
      Top k

      One choice

      Dowry problems

A useful way to generate new secretary problems is therefore to modify one or more components of the classical model:

  Information
  +
  Objective
  +
  Choice structure
  +
  Horizon

Each modification can produce a genuinely different optimal-stopping problem.

title: Secretary Problem Simulations
text:
What the experiments show
The simulations illustrate three important facts:

A nonrecord candidate cannot be the overall best.
Rejecting too few candidates provides insufficient information.
Rejecting too many candidates leaves too few opportunities to select a later record.

The optimal threshold balances these competing risks.
For large (n),
\[
r^\star\approx \frac{n}{e},
\qquad
P_n(r^\star)\approx\frac1e.
\]
Therefore, both the optimal rejection fraction and the maximum success probability approach approximately (37%).






NoteSimulation versus proof



Monte Carlo simulation provides numerical evidence, but it does not prove optimality. The exact probability formula and the backward-induction argument establish the mathematical result.

title: Classical Secretary Problem: Proof and the 37% Rule
text:
Why should you reject roughly the first 37% of candidates before choosing? The secretary problem is a classical optimal stopping problem: decisions are sequential, rejections are final, and success means selecting the single best candidate.
The exact finite-sample solution and its asymptotic 37% rule are derived below; you can also experiment with the rule.

title: Classical Secretary Problem: Proof and the 37% Rule
text:
The question in plain language
Suppose you interview 100 candidates in random order. After each interview, you know how that candidate compares with the people you have already met—but not how they compare with candidates you have not seen. You must decide immediately whether to hire them or reject them forever.
Would you hire a strong early candidate, or wait and risk losing everyone?
The classical strategy has two phases:

Observe: Reject an initial group and note the best candidate in that group.
Choose: Hire the first later candidate who is better than everyone interviewed so far. If no such candidate appears, you do not succeed.

For a large pool of candidates, the best observation period is approximately 37% of the total. With 100 candidates, that suggests observing about 37 first; the exact best integer cutoff comes from the finite-sample mathematics below.
This result depends on the assumptions of the model. It is not a universal recommendation for real hiring, dating, or investment decisions.
Try hiring candidates yourself →

title: Classical Secretary Problem: Proof and the 37% Rule
text:
Model and assumptions
There are \(n\ge 2\) candidates, ranked absolutely from \(1\) (best) to \(n\) (worst). The classical no-information model assumes:

The candidates arrive in a uniformly random order (all \(n!\) orders are equally likely).
You observe only each candidate’s relative rank among those seen so far, not their absolute rank.
You may accept at most one candidate. Every rejection is irrevocable.
Your objective is to maximize the probability of choosing the single overall best candidate.

A candidate is a record if they are better than all candidates seen before. Since a nonrecord cannot be the overall best, there is no benefit to selecting one when the objective is the overall best.

title: Classical Secretary Problem: Proof and the 37% Rule
text:
The threshold strategy
Fix an integer \(r\) with \(0\le r<n\):

Reject the first \(r\) candidates, observing their relative ranks.
Starting at position \(r+1\), accept the first record (a candidate better than every earlier candidate).
If there is no subsequent record, no candidate is selected and the attempt fails. (Requiring a selection at the final interview would not change the probability of selecting the overall best.)

For \(r=0\), the rule accepts the first candidate immediately. This convention is used in the interactive simulation below.
The classical theorem establishes that a threshold rule is optimal among all stopping rules based on relative ranks, not merely the best rule within a preselected class of thresholds. A backward-induction proof of this optimal-policy structure is provided on the Backward Induction page.

title: Classical Secretary Problem: Proof and the 37% Rule
section: Exact success probability: a finite-\(n\) derivation
text:
Exact success probability: a finite-\(n\) derivation
Let \(P_n(r)\) denote the probability that the threshold-\(r\) strategy selects absolute rank \(1\).
Proposition. For \(1\le r<n\),
\[
\boxed{
P_n(r)=\frac{r}{n}\sum_{k=r+1}^{n}\frac{1}{k-1}
=\frac{r}{n}\left(H_{n-1}-H_{r-1}\right),
}
\]
where \(H_m=\sum_{j=1}^m 1/j\) for \(m\ge1\) and \(H_0=0\). For \(r=0\), \(P_n(0)=1/n\).
Proof. Write \(K\) for the arrival position of the overall best candidate. Uniform random order gives
\[
\Pr(K=k)=\frac1n,\qquad k=1,\ldots,n.
\]
If \(K\le r\), that candidate is rejected, so success is impossible. If \(K=k>r\), the strategy selects the overall best precisely when the best candidate among the first \(k-1\) arrivals occurred during the initial \(r\) positions. Otherwise, a record after position \(r\) would have triggered selection earlier.
Conditionally on \(K=k\), each of the first \(k-1\) positions is equally likely to hold the best among those first \(k-1\) candidates. Thus
\[
\Pr(\text{success}\mid K=k)=\frac{r}{k-1},\qquad k>r.
\]
Summing over the possible positions of the overall best gives
\[
P_n(r)
=\sum_{k=r+1}^{n}\Pr(K=k)\Pr(\text{success}\mid K=k)
=\frac{r}{n}\sum_{k=r+1}^{n}\frac{1}{k-1}.
\]
If \(r=0\), the first candidate is accepted, which is the overall best with probability \(1/n\). \(\square\)

title: Classical Secretary Problem: Proof and the 37% Rule
section: Which threshold is optimal for a given \(n\)?
text:
Which threshold is optimal for a given \(n\)?
Finite-\(n\) criterion. For \(1\le r<n-1\),
\[
\boxed{
P_n(r+1)-P_n(r)
=\frac1n\left(\sum_{j=r+1}^{n-1}\frac1j-1\right).
}
\]
To see this, subtract the two formulas:
\[
\begin{aligned}
nP_n(r+1)&=(r+1)\sum_{j=r+1}^{n-1}\frac1j,\\
nP_n(r)&=1+r\sum_{j=r+1}^{n-1}\frac1j.
\end{aligned}
\]
The sum in the difference decreases strictly as \(r\) increases. Consequently, the threshold probabilities increase while the sum exceeds \(1\), are equal at adjacent thresholds if the sum equals \(1\), and decrease once the sum falls below \(1\).
The boundary case \(r=0\) must be considered separately: for \(n\ge3\), \(P_n(1)=H_{n-1}/n>1/n=P_n(0)\), whereas for \(n=2\) the two probabilities are equal. Thus, for \(n\ge3\), the smallest optimal threshold is
\[
\boxed{
r_n^\star=\min\left\{r\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}:
\sum_{j=r+1}^{n-1}\frac1j\le1\right\}.
}
\]
An empty sum is \(0\). If the sum equals \(1\) at the transition and \(r_n^\star<n-1\), the adjacent threshold \(r_n^\star+1\) is also optimal. For \(n=2\), both \(r=0\) and \(r=1\) have success probability \(1/2\).
For example, with \(n=10\), the optimal threshold is \(r^\star=3\), and
\[
P_{10}(3)=\frac3{10}\left(\frac13+\frac14+\cdots+\frac19\right)\approx0.39869.
\]
This exact threshold need not equal the integer obtained by simply rounding \(n/e\).

title: Classical Secretary Problem: Proof and the 37% Rule
text:
Why the 37% rule appears
Suppose \(n\) grows and \(r/n\to x\in(0,1)\). The harmonic sum satisfies
\[
\sum_{j=r}^{n-1}\frac1j
=\log\left(\frac nr\right)+o(1),
\]
so
\[
P_n(r)=\frac rn\sum_{j=r}^{n-1}\frac1j
\longrightarrow -x\log x.
\]
Differentiating yields
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[-x\log x]=-\log x-1.
\]
This vanishes at \(x=e^{-1}\), where the second derivative \(-1/x\) is negative. The finite-\(n\) optimality criterion above also implies that \(r_n^\star/n\to 1/e\). Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\frac{r_n^\star}{n}\longrightarrow\frac1e,
\qquad
P_n(r_n^\star)\longrightarrow\frac1e
\approx 0.367879.
}
\]
Interpretation: for a large pool, reject about 36.8% of candidates, then accept the next record. The limiting probability of choosing the best is also about 36.8%. These are two distinct quantities that happen to share the same limit; for a fixed finite \(n\), they generally differ.

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
This page derives the optimal policy from first principles using the value equation
\[
V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\}.
\]
Here, \(U_n\) is the value of stopping at a record, \(W_n\) is the value of continuing, and \(V_n\) is the optimal value.

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
This page derives the optimal policy from first principles using the value equation
\[
V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\}.
\]
Here, \(U_n\) is the value of stopping at a record, \(W_n\) is the value of continuing, and \(V_n\) is the optimal value.

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
1. Model and objective
There are \(N\ge3\) candidates arriving in a uniformly random order. Their absolute ranks are
\[
1,2,\ldots,N,
\]
where rank \(1\) is best.
After interviewing a candidate, we observe only that candidate’s rank relative to those already seen. An accepted candidate ends the process, and a rejected candidate cannot be recalled.
Let \(X_k\) be the absolute rank of the candidate in position \(k\). We seek a stopping time \(\tau\) maximizing
\[
\mathbb P(X_\tau=1).
\]
Thus, the reward is \(1\) if the selected candidate is the overall best and \(0\) otherwise.

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
2. Relative ranks and records
Define the relative rank of the candidate in position \(n\) by
\[
R_n
=
1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}
\mathbf 1_{\{X_j<X_n\}}.
\]
The event \(R_n=1\) means that the candidate at time \(n\) is better than every candidate previously observed.
Such a candidate is called a record.
A non-record cannot be the overall best. It is therefore always optimal to continue at a non-record while further candidates remain. The only decisions that can offer a positive chance of success from stopping occur when \(R_n=1\).

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
3. Uniformity of relative ranks






NoteRelative-rank theorem



For a uniformly random permutation, the relative ranks
\[
R_1,R_2,\ldots,R_N
\]
are independent. Moreover,
\[
\mathbb P(R_n=j)=\frac1n,
\qquad
j=1,\ldots,n.
\]
In particular,
\[
\mathbb P(R_n=1)=\frac1n.
\]



Proof
The transformation from the absolute-rank permutation
\[
(X_1,\ldots,X_N)
\]
to the relative-rank sequence
\[
(R_1,\ldots,R_N)
\]
is a bijection.
Every admissible relative-rank sequence satisfies
\[
R_n\in\{1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
The number of such sequences is
\[
1\cdot2\cdots N=N!,
\]
which equals the number of absolute-rank permutations.
Because all absolute-rank permutations are equally likely, every admissible relative-rank sequence has probability \(1/N!\). Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(R_1=r_1,\ldots,R_N=r_N)
&=\frac1{N!}\\
&=\prod_{n=1}^{N}\frac1n.
\end{aligned}
\]
This factorization proves that the relative ranks are independent and that each \(R_n\) is uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). \(\square\)

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
4. The value of stopping
Suppose the candidate at time \(n\) is a record.
Since the overall best candidate is necessarily a record,
\[
\mathbb P(X_n=1,\ R_n=1)
=
\mathbb P(X_n=1)
=
\frac1N.
\]
By the relative-rank theorem,
\[
\mathbb P(R_n=1)=\frac1n.
\]
Therefore, the probability of success from stopping at a record at time \(n\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_n
&=
\mathbb P(X_n=1\mid R_n=1)\\
&=
\frac{\mathbb P(X_n=1,\ R_n=1)}
     {\mathbb P(R_n=1)}\\
&=
\frac{1/N}{1/n}\\
&=
\frac nN.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence,
\[
\boxed{U_n=\frac nN}.
\]
The stopping value is strictly increasing in \(n\).

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
5. The continuation value
Let \(W_n\) be the optimal conditional probability of eventual success after rejecting the candidate at time \(n\), given the relative-rank observations available at that time. By independence of the successive relative ranks, this value depends on \(n\) but not on the previously observed relative ranks.
At a record time, define
\[
\boxed{V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\}}.
\]
At time \(n+1\), the next candidate is a record with probability
\[
\frac1{n+1}.
\]
If a new record appears, another stop-or-continue decision is available and the value is \(V_{n+1}\).
With probability
\[
\frac n{n+1},
\]
the candidate is not a record. Stopping cannot then produce success, so the process continues with value \(W_{n+1}\).
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
W_n
=
\frac{1}{n+1}V_{n+1}
+
\frac{n}{n+1}W_{n+1}
}.
\]
The Bellman equations are therefore
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
U_n&=\frac nN,\\
V_n&=\max\{U_n,W_n\},\\
W_n&=
\frac{1}{n+1}V_{n+1}
+
\frac{n}{n+1}W_{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
6. Terminal condition
At time \(N\), accepting a record wins with certainty. There is no remaining opportunity to succeed after rejection. If a selection at time \(N\) is mandatory, selecting a non-record yields reward zero and does not affect the value.
Therefore,
\[
U_N=1,
\qquad
V_N=1,
\qquad
W_N=0.
\]
Starting with these terminal values, all preceding values are determined by backward induction.

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
section: 7. Why the optimal policy has one threshold
text:
7. Why the optimal policy has one threshold
From the continuation recurrence,
\[
W_n
=
\frac{1}{n+1}V_{n+1}
+
\frac{n}{n+1}W_{n+1}.
\]
Subtracting \(W_{n+1}\) gives
\[
W_n-W_{n+1}
=
\frac{V_{n+1}-W_{n+1}}{n+1}.
\]
Since
\[
V_{n+1}
=
\max\{U_{n+1},W_{n+1}\}
\ge W_{n+1},
\]
we obtain
\[
W_n-W_{n+1}\ge0.
\]
Thus,
\[
W_1\ge W_2\ge\cdots\ge W_N.
\]
The continuation value \(W_n\) is nonincreasing, while the stopping value
\[
U_n=\frac nN
\]
is strictly increasing.
Thus \(U_n-W_n\) is strictly increasing in \(n\). Once accepting a record is optimal, it remains optimal at every later record time. This proves that an optimal policy has a threshold form.
There is an integer \(r^*\) such that the optimal policy is:

Reject the first \(r^*\) candidates.
Beginning at position \(r^*+1\), accept the first record.
If no later record appears, the selection fails.

At a record time \(n\), stopping is optimal whenever
\[
U_n\ge W_n.
\]
If equality holds, either stopping or continuing is optimal. We break ties in favor of stopping.

text:
8. Complete example: (N=10)
We now solve the problem for \(N=10\) without assuming the threshold in advance.
Begin with
\[
U_{10}=1,
\qquad
V_{10}=1,
\qquad
W_{10}=0.
\]
Then work backward using
\[

=
\frac{1}{n+1}V_{n+1}
+

\]

\]
The optimal success probability is
\[

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
section: 9. Success probability of a fixed threshold
text:
9. Success probability of a fixed threshold
Fix
\[
r\in\{1,\ldots,N-1\}.
\]
Consider the policy that rejects the first \(r\) candidates and accepts the first subsequent record.
Suppose the overall best candidate occurs at position \(k>r\). The strategy selects that candidate precisely when the best among the first \(k-1\) candidates occurs during the initial rejection period.
The overall best is equally likely to occupy any position, so
\[
\mathbb P(X_k=1)=\frac1N.
\]
Conditional on \(X_k=1\), the best candidate among the first \(k-1\) positions is equally likely to occupy any of those positions. Therefore, the probability that it occurs among the first \(r\) positions is
\[
\frac{r}{k-1}.
\]
Summing over the possible positions of the overall best gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_N(r)
&=
\sum_{k=r+1}^{N}
\frac1N\frac{r}{k-1}\\
&=
\frac rN
\sum_{k=r+1}^{N}\frac1{k-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Changing the summation index yields
\[
\boxed{
P_N(r)
=
\frac rN
\sum_{j=r}^{N-1}\frac1j
}.
\]
If \(r=0\), the first candidate is accepted immediately, and
\[
P_N(0)=\frac1N.
\]






WarningDistinguishing (W_r) from (P_N(r))



The quantities \(W_r\) and \(P_N(r)\) have different meanings.
The value \(W_r\) is the probability of eventual success when all future decisions are made optimally after time \(r\).
In contrast, \(P_N(r)\) is the success probability of the fixed threshold-\(r\) strategy.
They are not necessarily equal.
For example, when \(N=10\),
\[
P_{10}(1)
=
\frac1{10}\sum_{j=1}^{9}\frac1j
\approx0.2829,
\]
whereas
\[
W_1
=
\frac{3349}{8400}
\approx0.3987.
\]
At the optimal threshold,
\[
\boxed{
W_{r^*}=P_N(r^*)=V_1
}.
\]

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
10. Exact characterization of the threshold
For \(r=1,\ldots,N-2\),
\[
P_N(r)
=
\frac rN
\sum_{j=r}^{N-1}\frac1j
\]
and
\[
P_N(r+1)
=
\frac{r+1}{N}
\sum_{j=r+1}^{N-1}\frac1j.
\]
Since
\[
P_N(r)
=
\frac rN
\left(
\frac1r+
\sum_{j=r+1}^{N-1}\frac1j
\right),
\]
subtraction gives
\[
\boxed{
P_N(r+1)-P_N(r)
=
\frac1N
\left(
\sum_{j=r+1}^{N-1}\frac1j-1
\right)
}.
\]
It follows that \(P_N(r)\) increases while
\[
\sum_{j=r+1}^{N-1}\frac1j>1
\]
and decreases after this sum becomes smaller than \(1\).
The smallest optimal threshold is
\[
\boxed{
r^*
=
\min
\left\{
r\in\{1,\ldots,N-1\}:
\sum_{j=r+1}^{N-1}\frac1j\le1
\right\}.
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\sum_{j=r^*+1}^{N-1}\frac1j
\le1
\le
\sum_{j=r^*}^{N-1}\frac1j.
}
\]
If the left-hand sum in the displayed characterization equals \(1\), two adjacent thresholds are optimal: \(r^*\) and \(r^*+1\). The definition above selects the smaller rejection threshold, consistent with breaking a decision tie in favor of stopping. The boundary case \(r=0\) is excluded for \(N\ge3\), because \(P_N(1)=H_{N-1}/N>1/N=P_N(0)\).

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
11. The asymptotic (1/e) rule
For large \(N\), the harmonic sum can be approximated by an integral:
\[
\sum_{j=r+1}^{N-1}\frac1j
\approx
\int_r^N\frac{dx}{x}
=
\log\frac Nr.
\]
The threshold condition is therefore approximately
\[
\log\frac N{r^*}=1.
\]
Solving for \(r^*\) gives
\[
\boxed{
\frac{r^*}{N}\longrightarrow\frac1e
}.
\]
Using the exact probability formula,
\[
P_N(r^*)
=
\frac{r^*}{N}
\sum_{j=r^*}^{N-1}\frac1j.
\]
The first factor approaches \(1/e\), while the harmonic sum approaches \(1\). Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
P_N(r^*)\longrightarrow\frac1e
}.
\]
Numerically,
\[
\frac1e\approx0.367879.
\]






ImportantFinal result



For a large number of candidates:

Reject approximately the first \(N/e\) candidates.
Record the best candidate observed during that period.
Accept the first later candidate who is better than every previously observed candidate.

Both the optimal rejection fraction and the optimal success probability approach approximately \(37\%\).

title: Secretary Problem by Backward Induction
text:
12. General backward-induction theorem
The preceding calculation is a finite-horizon instance of the Snell-envelope theorem.
To distinguish the general theory from the secretary-specific notation, let \(G_n\) denote a general reward process and let \(Z_n\) denote its value process.






NoteTheorem: finite-horizon optimal stopping



Let
\[
G_1,G_2,\ldots,G_N
\]
be an integrable process adapted to a filtration
\[
\mathcal F_1,\mathcal F_2,\ldots,\mathcal F_N.
\]
Define
\[
Z_N=G_N
\]
and, for \(n=N-1,\ldots,1\), define
\[
\boxed{
Z_n
=
\max
\left\{
G_n,
\mathbb E[Z_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]
\right\}.
}
\]
Then
\[
Z_n
=
\mathop{\mathrm{ess\,sup}}_{\tau\in\mathcal T_{n,N}}
\mathbb E[G_\tau\mid\mathcal F_n],
\]
where \(\mathcal T_{n,N}\) is the collection of stopping times taking values in
\[
\{n,\ldots,N\}.
\]
An optimal stopping time beginning at time \(n\) is
\[
\boxed{
\tau_n^*
=
\inf
\{k\ge n:G_k=Z_k\}.
}
\]



Proof
At time \(N\), stopping is compulsory. Therefore,
\[
Z_N=G_N.
\]
Assume that \(Z_{n+1}\) is the optimal value beginning at time \(n+1\).
At time \(n\), there are two alternatives.
If we stop, the reward is \(G_n\).
If we continue, the best attainable conditional value is
\[
\mathbb E[Z_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n].
\]
The optimal value is therefore
\[
Z_n
=
\max
\left\{
G_n,
\mathbb E[Z_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]
\right\}.
\]
Backward induction proves the value formula at every time. Stopping at the first time when the immediate reward equals the value process attains this value. \(\square\)


Connection with the secretary problem
For the secretary problem, let \(\mathcal F_n=\sigma(R_1,\ldots,R_n)\) be the information available after the first \(n\) interviews. Define the \(\mathcal F_n\)-measurable reward for selecting the candidate at time \(n\) by
\[
G_n=\mathbb P(X_n=1\mid\mathcal F_n)
=\frac nN\,\mathbf 1_{\{R_n=1\}}.
\]
Indeed, a non-record cannot be the overall best; when \(R_n=1\), the conditional winning probability is \(n/N\). The independence of the relative ranks ensures that the previous observations do not alter this conditional probability.
Maximizing the expected conditional reward \(G_\tau\) is equivalent to maximizing \(\mathbb P(X_\tau=1)\), by the tower property. In particular, the compulsory-stopping formulation at \(N\) has the same optimal success probability as the formulation permitting no selection when no later record appears.
At a record time \(n\), the conditional reward of stopping is \(U_n=n/N\) and the value of continuing is \(W_n\). The Snell-envelope recursion therefore reduces to
\[
\boxed{V_n=\max\{U_n,W_n\}}
\]
at record times. At non-record times, stopping gives zero, so continuing is optimal whenever additional candidates remain. These are exactly the decisions used in the backward induction above.

The general theory of backward induction and optimal stopping is developed by Chow, Robbins, and Siegmund (1971), Shiryaev (2007), and Ferguson (2010).
Historical and foundational treatments of the secretary problem include Ferguson (1989) and Gilbert and Mosteller (1966).

title: The Secretary Problem Site
text:
About the subject
The secretary problem is a starting point for a family of optimal-stopping models. Different assumptions about the available information, number of choices, and objective lead to different mathematical questions.
Begin with the classical secretary problem, explore its exact optimal stopping rule, and experiment with interactive simulations. The site connects these ideas to variants and extensions and the research literature.

title: Secretary Problem Research Timeline
section: More than sixty years of optimal stopping
text:
More than sixty years of optimal stopping
The secretary problem developed from a recreational question into a major model in optimal stopping, applied probability, decision theory, economics, and online algorithms.

In Who Solved the Secretary Problem? (1989), Thomas S. Ferguson separates the problem’s early circulation from its publication and mathematical solution. Merrill Flood had discussed a version by 1950; Martin Gardner brought the problem to a wide audience in his February 1960 Scientific American column, drawing on a formulation attributed to John H. Fox Jr. and L. Gerald Marnie. Ferguson identifies D. V. Lindley’s 1961 paper as the first solution in a scientific journal. Gardner’s popularization and Lindley’s mathematical treatment are therefore distinct milestones in the history of the classical secretary problem.
